p.src: Now Cao Cao raised an army for a western campaign and divided it into three columns, with Xiahou Yuan and Zhang He commanding the vanguard. Cao Cao himself led the generals in the center. Cao Ren and Xiahou Dun brought up the rear, escorting the provisions and fodder. Spies soon carried word of this into Hanzhong. Zhang Lu and his younger brother Zhang Wei discussed how to repel the enemy. Zhang Wei said, “Of all the strongholds in Hanzhong, none is more formidable than Yangping Pass. On either side of the pass, against the mountains and beside the forests, we can establish more than ten fortified camps to meet Cao Cao’s army. You, brother, should remain in Hanning and send ample provisions to support us.”

p.src: Zhang Lu followed his advice and ordered the generals Yang Ang and Yang Ren to depart that very day with his brother. When their forces reached Yangping Pass, they established their camps. The vanguard under Xiahou Yuan and Zhang He arrived soon afterward. Learning that preparations had already been made at Yangping Pass, they encamped fifteen li away. That night the weary soldiers each settled down to rest. Suddenly fire broke out behind the camp, and the troops of Yang Ang and Yang Ren attacked from two directions to raid it. Xiahou Yuan and Zhang He hurriedly mounted, but enemy troops poured in from every side. Cao Cao’s forces suffered a crushing defeat and withdrew to report to him. Cao Cao angrily said, “You two have campaigned for many years. Do you not know that when troops are exhausted after a long march, the camp must be guarded against attack? Why did you make no preparations?” He intended to behead them both as a demonstration of military law. The assembled officers pleaded for their pardon.

p.src: The next day Cao Cao personally led the vanguard. Seeing the forbidding mountains, the tangled forests, and the unfamiliar paths, he feared an ambush and led his army back to camp. He said to the two generals Xu Chu and Xu Huang, “Had I known this place was so perilous, I would never have raised an army to come here.” Xu Chu said, “Our army has already come this far, my lord. You must not shrink from the toil.” The next day Cao Cao mounted, taking only Xu Chu and Xu Huang with him, and went to inspect Zhang Wei’s fortifications. As the three riders rounded a mountainside, Zhang Wei’s fortifications came into view. Cao Cao raised his whip and pointed into the distance, saying to the two generals, “With defenses this strong, it will be difficult to take them quickly!”

p.src: Before he had finished speaking, a great cry arose behind them and arrows fell like rain. Yang Ang and Yang Ren charged in from two directions. Cao Cao was greatly alarmed. Xu Chu shouted, “I will hold off the enemy! Gongming, protect our lord well!” With that, he raised his saber, spurred his horse forward, and fought the two generals with all his might. Yang Ang and Yang Ren could not withstand Xu Chu’s valor and turned their horses in retreat; the others dared not advance. Xu Huang escorted Cao Cao over the mountainside, but another force appeared ahead. Looking closely, they saw that it was Xiahou Yuan and Zhang He, who had heard the battle cries and brought troops to their aid. Together they drove back Yang Ang and Yang Ren and rescued Cao Cao, bringing him safely to camp. Cao Cao richly rewarded the four generals. Thereafter the two sides remained locked in opposition for more than fifty days without giving battle. Cao Cao gave orders to withdraw. Jia Xu asked, “The enemy’s true strength has not yet been revealed. Why does my lord withdraw of his own accord?” Cao Cao replied, “I judge that the enemy keeps vigilant guard every day, so it will be difficult to win quickly. I shall pretend to withdraw, causing the enemy to relax and leave themselves unprepared. Then I will divide my light cavalry and send them by a circuitous route to strike the enemy’s rear. Victory will be certain.” Jia Xu said, “The Chancellor’s divine strategy is truly unfathomable.”

p.src: Cao Cao therefore ordered Xiahou Yuan and Zhang He to divide their forces into two columns, each leading three thousand light cavalry along narrow paths to circle behind Yangping Pass. Meanwhile, Cao Cao led the main army in striking camp and withdrawing in full. When Yang Ang heard that Cao Cao’s army was retreating, he consulted Yang Ren and proposed attacking while they had the advantage. Yang Ren said, “Cao Cao has countless cunning schemes. We do not yet know whether this is genuine, so we must not pursue.” Yang Ang said, “If you will not go, I shall go myself.” Yang Ren earnestly remonstrated, but Yang Ang would not listen. Yang Ang led out all the troops from five camps, leaving only a small number of soldiers to guard them. That day a dense fog spread everywhere, so that no one could see even those directly before them. Halfway there, Yang Ang’s army could go no farther and halted temporarily.

p.src: Meanwhile, Xiahou Yuan’s column had circled behind the mountains. Seeing thick fog hanging over the land and hearing voices and horses neighing, he feared an ambush and urgently pressed his troops onward. In the dense fog, however, they mistakenly came to the front of Yang Ang’s camp. Hearing the sound of hoofbeats, the soldiers guarding the camp assumed that Yang Ang’s troops had returned and opened the gates to admit them. Cao Cao’s soldiers surged inside. Finding the camp nearly empty, they set it ablaze. The soldiers in all five camps abandoned their positions and fled. By the time the fog cleared, Yang Ren had led troops to the rescue. He had fought Xiahou Yuan for only a few bouts when Zhang He’s forces arrived behind him. Yang Ren fought his way through and fled back to Nanzheng. When Yang Ang sought to return, Xiahou Yuan and Zhang He had already occupied the fortifications. Behind him, Cao Cao’s main army came rushing in pursuit. Attacked from both sides, he had no path of escape in any direction. Yang Ang tried to break through the battle lines but ran straight into Zhang He. The two crossed weapons, and Zhang He slew him. The defeated soldiers fled back toward Yangping Pass to report to Zhang Wei. But Zhang Wei, learning that the two generals had been defeated and all the camps lost, had already abandoned the pass at midnight and fled back. Thus Cao Cao captured Yangping Pass and all its surrounding camps.

p.src: Zhang Wei and Yang Ren returned to see Zhang Lu. Zhang Wei said that the two generals had lost the strategic passes, making it impossible to hold Yangping Pass. Zhang Lu was furious and intended to behead Yang Ren. Yang Ren said, “I warned Yang Ang not to pursue Cao Cao’s army. He refused to listen, and that is why this defeat occurred. I beg for another army so that I may go forth and challenge the enemy. I shall certainly behead Cao Cao. If I fail to win, I will willingly submit to military punishment.” Zhang Lu accepted his written pledge under military law. Yang Ren mounted and led twenty thousand troops out of Nanzheng to establish camp.

p.src: Meanwhile, as Cao Cao prepared to advance, he first ordered Xiahou Yuan to take five thousand soldiers and scout the road to Nanzheng. They encountered Yang Ren’s army head-on, and the two forces drew up their battle lines. Yang Ren sent his subordinate commander Chang Qi to ride out and engage Xiahou Yuan. Before three bouts had passed, Xiahou Yuan cut him down from his horse with a single stroke. Yang Ren himself rode out with leveled spear and fought Xiahou Yuan for more than thirty bouts, neither gaining the advantage. Xiahou Yuan feigned defeat and fled, and Yang Ren pursued him from behind. Xiahou Yuan used the trailing-saber stratagem and cut him down from his horse. His soldiers suffered a great defeat and fled back.

p.src: When Cao Cao learned that Xiahou Yuan had slain Yang Ren, he immediately advanced and encamped directly outside Nanzheng. In alarm, Zhang Lu assembled his civil and military officials for counsel. Yan Pu said, “I recommend one man who can stand against all the generals under Cao Cao.” Zhang Lu asked who it was. Yan Pu replied, “Pang De of Nan’an formerly followed Ma Chao and later submitted to my lord. When Ma Chao later went to the Western Riverlands, Pang De was ill and could not accompany him. He now receives my lord’s gracious support. Why not send him?”

p.src: Zhang Lu was delighted. He summoned Pang De at once and rewarded him generously. He mustered ten thousand troops and ordered Pang De to march out. More than ten li from the city, Pang De faced Cao Cao’s army and rode forward to issue a challenge. Cao Cao had witnessed Pang De’s valor at the Wei Bridge and therefore instructed his generals, “Pang De is a valiant warrior of Xiliang and formerly served Ma Chao. Though he now depends upon Zhang Lu, his heart is not satisfied there. I wish to obtain this man. Each of you must fight him at a measured pace until his strength is spent, and then we shall capture him.”

p.src: Zhang He rode out first, fought a few bouts, and then withdrew. Xiahou Yuan also fought several bouts and withdrew. Xu Huang fought another three or five bouts and likewise withdrew. Finally, Xu Chu fought for more than fifty bouts before he too withdrew. Pang De fought all four generals fiercely without showing the slightest fear. Each general praised Pang De’s superb martial skill before Cao Cao. Cao Cao was delighted and consulted his generals, saying, “How can we induce this man to surrender?” Jia Xu said, “I know that Zhang Lu has an adviser named Yang Song under him. The man is exceedingly greedy for bribes. We can secretly send him gold and silk and have him slander Pang De before Zhang Lu. Then our aim can be achieved.” Cao Cao asked, “How can anyone get into Nanzheng?” Jia Xu replied, “In tomorrow’s battle we shall feign defeat, abandon our camp, and flee, allowing Pang De to occupy it. Then, in the dead of night, we shall lead troops back to raid the camp. Pang De will certainly retreat into the city. We can then choose an eloquent soldier, disguise him as one of Pang De’s men, and mingle him among their ranks; in that way he will be able to enter the city.”

p.src: Cao Cao accepted his plan and selected a shrewd soldier, rewarding him generously and giving him a golden breastplate to wear next to his skin. Over it he put on the uniform of a Hanzhong soldier and went ahead to wait along the road. The next day he first sent the two forces of Xiahou Yuan and Zhang He to lie in ambush far away; then he ordered Xu Huang to issue a challenge and feign defeat after only a few bouts. Pang De called his troops forward in pursuit, and Cao Cao's soldiers all withdrew. Pang De then seized Cao Cao's stockade. Seeing the great quantity of grain and fodder in the camp, he rejoiced and immediately reported the victory to Zhang Lu; at the same time, he held a banquet in the camp to celebrate.

p.src: That night, after the second watch, fires suddenly arose from three directions: in the center were Xu Huang and Xu Chu; on the left was Zhang He; and on the right, Xiahou Yuan. The troops from all three directions attacked the camp together. Caught unprepared, Pang De could only mount his horse, fight his way out, and flee toward the city. The three forces pursued him from behind. Pang De at once called for the gates to be opened and led his soldiers surging into the city.

p.src: By then the spy had slipped into the city among the troops. He went straight to Yang Song's residence and, on being admitted, explained everything: “The Duke of Wei, Chancellor Cao, has long heard of your eminent virtue and has specially sent me to present this golden armor as a token. I also have a secret letter to present.” Yang Song was delighted. After reading the words in the secret letter, he told the spy, “Report to the Duke of Wei that he need only set his mind at ease. I have an excellent plan with which to answer him.” He dismissed the messenger to return first, then went that very night to see Zhang Lu and claimed that Pang De had accepted Cao Cao's bribe and deliberately thrown the battle. Zhang Lu flew into a rage, summoned Pang De, berated him, and intended to have him beheaded. Yan Pu remonstrated with him earnestly. Zhang Lu said, “Go out to battle tomorrow. If you do not win, you will certainly be beheaded!” Pang De withdrew, nursing bitter resentment.

p.src: The next day Cao Cao's troops attacked the city, and Pang De led his soldiers charging out. Cao Cao ordered Xu Chu to engage him. Xu Chu feigned defeat, and Pang De pursued him. From horseback on a hillside Cao Cao called out, “Pang Lingming, why did you not surrender sooner?” Pang De thought, “To capture Cao Cao would be worth a thousand great generals!” He spurred his horse and raced up the slope. At a sudden shout, it seemed heaven and earth collapsed: horse and rider together plunged into a pitfall; men armed with hooks and ropes rushed in from every side, captured Pang De alive, and escorted him up the slope. Cao Cao dismounted, ordered the soldiers back, personally untied Pang De's bonds, and asked whether he would surrender. Reflecting on Zhang Lu's cruelty, Pang De willingly bowed and surrendered. Cao Cao personally helped him onto a horse, and they returned together to the main camp, deliberately allowing the men on the city walls to see them. Someone reported to Zhang Lu that Pang De and Cao Cao were riding side by side. Zhang Lu now believed all the more that Yang Song's accusation was true.

p.src: The next day Cao Cao raised scaling ladders on three sides and assailed the city with stone-throwing engines. Seeing that the situation had become desperate, Zhang Lu consulted his younger brother Zhang Wei. Zhang Wei said, “Set fire to all the granaries and treasuries, then flee to the southern mountains and defend Bazhong.” Yang Song said, “It would be better to open the gates and surrender.” Zhang Lu hesitated, unable to decide. Zhang Wei said, “Simply burn everything and leave.” Zhang Lu said, “I had long intended to submit myself to the court, but had not yet found a way to convey my purpose; now I am forced to flee, but the granaries and treasuries belong to the state and must not be destroyed.” He therefore had them all sealed and locked.

p.src: That night, during the second watch, Zhang Lu took his entire household, old and young, opened the southern gate, and fought his way out. Cao Cao ordered that he not be pursued and led his army into Nanzheng; when he saw that Zhang Lu had sealed the storehouses, he thought highly of him and sent men to Bazhong to persuade him to surrender. Zhang Lu wished to surrender, but Zhang Wei refused. Yang Song secretly wrote to Cao Cao, urging him to advance and promising to act as his agent within the city. On receiving the letter, Cao Cao personally led his troops toward Bazhong. Zhang Lu sent his brother Zhang Wei to lead the troops against him, and Zhang Wei crossed weapons with Xu Chu; Xu Chu cut him down beneath his horse. The defeated troops returned and reported to Zhang Lu, who wished to hold fast to the city. Yang Song said, “If you do not go out now, you will merely sit here awaiting death. I will defend the city, while my lord should personally go and fight a battle to the death.”

Before the armies had even engaged, his rear ranks were already fleeing. Zhang Lu hurriedly retreated, with Cao Cao's troops pursuing from behind. When Zhang Lu reached the city walls, Yang Song closed the gates and refused him entry. With nowhere left to go, Zhang Lu was overtaken by Cao Cao, who shouted, “Why did you not surrender sooner?” Zhang Lu dismounted and prostrated himself in surrender. Yang Song alone had betrayed his lord in pursuit of glory, so Cao Cao ordered him beheaded in the marketplace as a warning to all.
A later poet lamented in verse:

p.src: Cao Cao had now taken Eastern Chuan. His registrar Sima Yi stepped forward and said, “Liu Bei took Liu Zhang's domain through deceit and force, and the people of Shu have not yet given him their allegiance. Now that my lord has gained Hanzhong, Yizhou is trembling. If you advance swiftly and attack, they are certain to crumble. The wise value the timely seizure of opportunity; this moment must not be lost.” Cao Cao sighed and said, “The trouble with men is that they never know contentment. Having gained Long, must one now covet Shu as well?” Liu Ye said, “Sima Zhongda's words are correct. If there is even a slight delay, Zhuge Liang, skilled in governing a state, will serve as chancellor, while Guan Yu, Zhang Fei, and the others, whose valor surpasses the whole army, will command as generals. Once the people of Shu are settled and the passes securely held, the land will be impossible to assail.” Cao Cao said, “The soldiers are weary from their long marches; for the present they should be allowed to rest and recover.” He therefore held his troops in place and made no move.

p.src: Now the people of Western Chuan, hearing that Cao Cao had taken Eastern Chuan and reckoning that he would certainly come for Western Chuan next, were seized by panic several times in a single day. Xuande summoned his military adviser to discuss the matter. Kongming said, “I have a plan that will make Cao Cao withdraw of his own accord.” Xuande asked what the plan was. Kongming said, “Cao Cao has stationed part of his army at Hefei because he fears Sun Quan. If we now return the three commanderies of Jiangxia, Changsha, and Guiyang to Wu and send an eloquent man to explain the advantages and dangers, persuading Wu to raise an army and strike Hefei, Cao Cao's position will be unsettled and he will surely turn his forces southward.” Xuande asked, “Who can serve as envoy?” Yi Ji said, “I am willing to go.” Xuande was delighted. He wrote a letter, prepared the proper gifts, and ordered Yi Ji to go first to Jingzhou and inform Yunchang, then proceed into Wu. On reaching Moling, Yi Ji went to see Sun Quan and first sent in his name. Sun Quan summoned Yi Ji inside. After Yi Ji had completed his formal salutations, Sun Quan asked, “Why have you come here?” Yi Ji replied, “Recently Zhuge Ziyu came to take possession of Changsha and the other two commanderies. As our military adviser was absent, the transfer was not properly completed, so I have now brought a letter returning them. We had also intended to return Nanjun and Lingling in Jingzhou; but Cao Cao's sudden seizure of Eastern Chuan has left General Guan with nowhere to establish himself. Hefei is now weakly defended. We hope that Your Lordship will raise an army and attack it, forcing Cao Cao to withdraw his forces southward. Once my lord has taken Eastern Chuan, he will return all of Jingzhou.” Sun Quan said, “Return for now to your lodging and allow me to deliberate.”

p.src: After Yi Ji withdrew, Sun Quan asked his advisers for a plan. Zhang Zhao said, “Liu Bei has devised this scheme because he fears Cao Cao will take Western Chuan. Even so, while Cao Cao is now in Hanzhong, taking advantage of the situation to seize Hefei would also be an excellent plan.” Sun Quan followed his advice. After sending Yi Ji back to Shu, he at once discussed raising an army against Cao Cao: he ordered Lu Su to receive the three commanderies of Changsha, Jiangxia, and Guiyang and station troops at Lukou; he recalled Lü Meng and Gan Ning; and also sent to Yuhang to recall Ling Tong.

p.src: Before many days had passed, Lü Meng and Gan Ning arrived first. Lü Meng proposed a plan: “Cao Cao has now ordered Zhu Guang, Governor of Lujiang, to station troops at Wan Castle, open extensive rice fields, and send grain to Hefei to provision the army. We should first seize Wan Castle and then attack Hefei.” Sun Quan said, “This plan accords perfectly with my wishes.” He therefore appointed Lü Meng and Gan Ning as the vanguard; Jiang Qin and Pan Zhang as the rearguard; and Sun Quan himself led Zhou Tai, Chen Wu, Dong Xi, and Xu Sheng in the central force. At the time, Cheng Pu, Huang Gai, and Han Dang were guarding various places and none accompanied the expedition.

p.src: Now the army crossed the river, took Hezhou, and marched straight to Wan Castle. Zhu Guang, Governor of Wan Castle, sent men to Hefei to request aid; meanwhile, he held the city fast behind its walls and refused to come out. When Sun Quan personally approached the walls to inspect them, arrows poured down like rain and struck his commander's canopy. Sun Quan returned to camp and asked his generals, “How are we to take Wan Castle?” Dong Xi said, “We can order the soldiers to raise an earthen mound and attack from it.” Xu Sheng said, “We can erect scaling ladders and construct elevated bridges, look down into the city, and attack it.” Lü Meng said, “Both methods will take many days to complete. Once reinforcements arrive from Hefei, the city will be beyond our grasp. Our army has only just arrived and its spirit is at its keenest; we must seize upon that vigor and attack with all our strength. Let us advance at daybreak tomorrow, and the city should fall by noon.”

p.src: Sun Quan followed his advice. The next day, after the troops had eaten at the fifth watch, the whole army advanced. Arrows and stones rained down together from the walls. Gan Ning, gripping an iron chain, pressed forward through the arrows and stones. Zhu Guang ordered all his crossbowmen to shoot. Gan Ning swept aside the thicket of arrows and felled Zhu Guang with one blow of his chain. Lü Meng beat the war drum in person. The soldiers surged forward as one and hacked Zhu Guang to death with their blades. Most of the remaining defenders surrendered, and Wan Castle was taken while it was still only the hour of the dragon. Zhang Liao was leading his army to the rescue when, halfway there, a scout rode back to report that Wan Castle had already fallen. Zhang Liao immediately turned his troops back to Hefei.

p.src: Sun Quan entered Wan Castle, and Ling Tong also arrived with his troops. After commending them, Sun Quan lavishly rewarded the whole army, bestowed rich gifts upon Lü Meng, Gan Ning, and the other generals, and held a banquet to celebrate their victory. Lü Meng yielded the seat of honor to Gan Ning and warmly praised his achievement. When the wine had begun to take effect, Ling Tong recalled his father's murder at Gan Ning's hands. Seeing Lü Meng praise him as well, he grew furious. After glaring fixedly for a long while, he suddenly drew the sword worn by an attendant, stepped into the banquet, and said, “There is no entertainment at this feast. Watch me perform a sword dance.” Gan Ning understood his intent. Shoving aside the banquet table, he rose, seized two halberds in both hands, tucked them firmly beneath his arms, and strode forward, saying, “Then watch me wield my halberds before the feast.” Lü Meng saw that neither man meant well; so he took a shield in one hand and a saber in the other, stood between them, and said, “Able though you both are, neither can match my skill.” With that, he began a saber-and-shield dance and forced the two men apart to opposite sides.

p.src: Someone had already gone to report the matter to Sun Quan. Sun Quan hastily mounted and rode straight to the banquet. Only when the generals saw Sun Quan arrive did they each lower their weapons. Sun Quan said, “I have always told you both to put aside your old enmity. Why have you behaved like this again today?” Ling Tong fell to the ground, weeping, and bowed before him. Sun Quan repeatedly admonished and restrained him. The next day, he raised his army to advance upon Hefei, and all three divisions set out.

p.src: After losing Wan Castle, Zhang Liao returned to Hefei, deeply troubled at heart. Suddenly, Cao Cao dispatched Xue Ti with a wooden box bearing Cao Cao's seal. On its side were written the words: “Open only when the enemy comes.” That day a report came: “Sun Quan is personally leading an army of a hundred thousand to attack Hefei.” Zhang Liao then opened the box and examined its contents. Inside was written: “If Sun Quan arrives, Generals Zhang and Li are to go out and fight; General Yue is to defend the city.” Zhang Liao showed the written order to Li Dian and Yue Jin. Yue Jin asked, “What is your judgment, General?” Zhang Liao replied, “Our lord is away on a distant campaign, and the troops of Wu believe they are certain to defeat us. We must now send troops out to meet them, fight with all our strength, and blunt their keen edge so as to steady our men's hearts. Only then can we hold the city.”

p.src: Li Dian had long been on bad terms with Zhang Liao. Hearing these words, he remained silent and gave no answer. Seeing that Li Dian said nothing, Yue Jin observed, “The enemy is many and we are few. It will be difficult to meet them in battle; we had better hold fast.” Zhang Liao said, “You gentlemen are thinking only of private feelings and disregarding public duty. I shall go out alone to meet the enemy and fight them to the death.” He at once ordered his attendants to prepare his horse. Li Dian rose resolutely and said, “If you are thus resolved, General, how could I dare forget public duty because of a private grievance? I am ready to obey your command.” Zhang Liao was delighted. “Since Mancheng is willing to assist me, tomorrow lead a force into ambush north of Xiaoyao Ford; when the Wu troops charge past, first cut down Xiaoshi Bridge, and Yue Wenqian and I will strike them.” Li Dian accepted the order and went off to muster his troops for the ambush.

p.src: Now Sun Quan ordered Lü Meng and Gan Ning to form the vanguard, while he and Ling Tong occupied the center. The remaining generals advanced one after another, driving toward Hefei. As the vanguard under Lü Meng and Gan Ning advanced, it met Yue Jin head-on. Gan Ning rode out and engaged Yue Jin. After only a few exchanges, Yue Jin feigned defeat and fled. Gan Ning called to Lü Meng, and together they led their troops in pursuit. Sun Quan, in the second division, heard that the vanguard had won and urged his troops onward. When they reached north of Xiaoyao Ford, a rapid succession of cannon blasts suddenly sounded. Zhang Liao's force attacked from the left, and Li Dian's from the right. Sun Quan was greatly alarmed and hurriedly ordered men to summon Lü Meng and Gan Ning back to his aid, but Zhang Liao's troops were already upon him. Ling Tong had only a little over three hundred horsemen under him, far too few to withstand the Cao army as it crashed down like a mountain. Ling Tong shouted, “My lord, why do you not cross Xiaoshi Bridge at once?”

p.src: Before he had finished speaking, Zhang Liao charged to the fore with more than two thousand horsemen. Ling Tong wheeled around and fought desperately. Sun Quan spurred his horse onto the bridge, but more than ten feet of its southern end had already been dismantled, without a single plank remaining. Sun Quan was so startled that he knew not what to do. His subordinate officer Gu Li shouted, “My lord, draw your horse back, then send it forward again and leap across the gap!” Sun Quan backed his horse more than thirty feet, then loosened the reins and applied the whip. With a single bound, the horse flew across to the southern side of the bridge. A later poet wrote:

p.src: After Sun Quan had leapt to the southern side of the bridge, Xu Sheng and Dong Xi came to meet him by boat. Ling Tong and Gu Li held Zhang Liao at bay. Gan Ning and Lü Meng led their troops back to the rescue, but Yue Jin pursued them from behind while Li Dian cut them off and engaged them. More than half the Wu troops were lost. All of the more than three hundred men under Ling Tong's command were slain. Ling Tong himself suffered several spear wounds. He fought his way to the bridge, but finding it broken, fled by circling along the river. Sun Quan saw him from the boat and urgently ordered Dong Xi to row over and take him aboard, enabling him to cross back safely. Lü Meng and Gan Ning likewise escaped for their lives to the southern bank. This battle struck terror into every heart south of the Yangtze; at the mere sound of Zhang Liao's great name, even children dared not cry at night. The generals escorted Sun Quan back to camp. Sun Quan richly rewarded Ling Tong and Gu Li, withdrew his army to Ruxu, readied the ships, and discussed a combined advance by land and water; at the same time, he sent men back south of the Yangtze to raise more troops for the campaign.

We would do better to withdraw our troops, relieve the peril at Hefei, and then descend upon the southlands.”
